The **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**, also known as the **Seven Wonders of the World** or simply the **Seven Wonders**, is a list of seven notable structures present during [classical antiquity](Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity"). The first known list of seven wonders dates back to the 2nd–1st century BC.

While the entries have varied over the centuries, the seven traditional wonders are the [Great Pyramid of Giza](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza "Great Pyramid of Giza"), the [Colossus of Rhodes](Colossus_of_Rhodes "Colossus of Rhodes"), the [Lighthouse of Alexandria](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria "Lighthouse of Alexandria"), the [Mausoleum at Halicarnassus](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus "Mausoleum at Halicarnassus"), the [Temple of Artemis](Temple_of_Artemis "Temple of Artemis"), the [Statue of Zeus at Olympia](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia "Statue of Zeus at Olympia"), and the [Hanging Gardens of Babylon](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon "Hanging Gardens of Babylon"). Using modern-day countries, two of the wonders were located in Greece, two in Turkey, two in Egypt, and one in Iraq. Of the seven wonders, only the Pyramid of Giza, which is also by far the oldest of the wonders, still remains standing, with the others being destroyed over the centuries. There is scholarly debate over the exact nature of the Hanging Gardens, and there is doubt as to whether they existed at all.

## Background

[Alexander the Great](Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great")'s conquest of much of the western world in the 4th century BC gave Hellenistic travellers access to the [civilizations](Civilization "Civilization") of the [Egyptians](Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt"), [Persians](History_of_Iran "History of Iran"), and [Babylonians](Babylonia "Babylonia").[[1]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-seven_wonders-1) Impressed and captivated by the landmarks and marvels of the various lands, these travellers began to list what they saw to remember them.[[2]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-history-2)[[3]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-seven-3)

Instead of "wonders", the ancient Greeks spoke of "*theamata*" (θεάματα), which means "sights", in other words "things to be seen" (Τὰ ἑπτὰ θεάματα τῆς οἰκουμένης [γῆς] **Tà heptà theámata tēs oikoumenēs [gēs]**). Later, the word for "wonder" ("*thaumata*" θαύματα, "wonders") was used.[[4]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-4) Hence, the list was meant to be the Ancient World's counterpart of a travel guidebook.[[1]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-seven_wonders-1)

The first reference to a list of seven such monuments was given by [Diodorus Siculus](Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus").[[5]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-5)[[6]](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World#cite_note-6) The epigra

The **Great Pyramid of Giza**[[lower-alpha 1]](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza#cite_note-3) is the largest [Egyptian pyramid](Egyptian_pyramid "Egyptian pyramid") and served as the tomb of [pharaoh](Pharaoh "Pharaoh") <Khufu>, who ruled during the [Fourth Dynasty](Fourth_Dynasty_of_Egypt "Fourth Dynasty of Egypt") of the [Old Kingdom](Old_Kingdom_of_Egypt "Old Kingdom of Egypt"). Built in the early 26th century BC, over a period of about 27 years,[[3]](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza#cite_note-FOOTNOTETallet2017-4) the pyramid is the oldest of the [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World"), and the only wonder that has remained largely intact. It is the most famous monument of the [Giza pyramid complex](Giza_pyramid_complex "Giza pyramid complex"), which is part of the [UNESCO World Heritage Site](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") "[Memphis](Memphis%2C_Egypt "Memphis, Egypt") and its [Necropolis](Memphite_Necropolis "Memphite Necropolis")".[[4]](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza#cite_note-:1-5) It is situated at the northern end of the line of the three pyramids at <Giza>.

Initially standing at 146.6 metres (481 feet), the Great Pyramid was the world's [tallest human-made structure](List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures#History "List of tallest buildings and structures") for more than 3,800 years. Over time, most of the smooth white [limestone](Limestone "Limestone") casing was removed, which lowered the pyramid's height to the current 138.5 metres (454.4 ft); what is seen today is the underlying core structure. The base was measured to be about 230.3 metres (755.6 ft) square, giving a volume of roughly 2.6 million cubic metres (92 million cubic feet), which includes an internal hillock.[[5]](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza#cite_note-FOOTNOTELehnerHawass2017143,_530–531-6)

The dimensions of the pyramid were 280 [royal cubits](Royal_cubit "Royal cubit") (146.7 m; 481.4 ft) high, a base length of 440 cubits (230.6 m; 756.4 ft), with a *[seked](Seked "Seked")* of 5+1/2 palms (a slope of 51°50'40").

It was built by quarrying an estimated 2.3 million large blocks, weighing 6 million tonnes in total. For other uses, see [Colossus of Rhodes (disambiguation)](Colossus_of_Rhodes_(disambiguation) "Colossus of Rhodes (disambiguation)").

The **Colossus of Rhodes** ([Ancient Greek](Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): ὁ Κολοσσὸς Ῥόδιος, [romanized](Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *ho Kolossòs Rhódios*; [Greek](Greek_language "Greek language"): Κολοσσός της Ρόδου, [romanized](Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"): *Kolossós tes Rhódou*)[[lower-alpha 1]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-2) was a [statue](Statue "Statue") of the Greek sun-god <Helios>, erected in the city of [Rhodes](Rhodes_(city) "Rhodes (city)"), on the Greek [island of the same name](Rhodes "Rhodes"), by [Chares of Lindos](Chares_of_Lindos "Chares of Lindos") in 280 BC. One of the [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World"), it was constructed to celebrate the successful defence of Rhodes city against an attack by [Demetrius I of Macedon](Demetrius_I_of_Macedon "Demetrius I of Macedon"), who had besieged it for a year with a large army and navy.

According to most contemporary descriptions, the Colossus stood approximately 70 [cubits](Cubit "Cubit"), or 33 metres (108 feet) high – approximately the height of the modern [Statue of Liberty](Statue_of_Liberty "Statue of Liberty") from feet to crown – making it the tallest statue in the [ancient world](Ancient_world "Ancient world").[[2]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-3) It collapsed during the [earthquake of 226 BC](226_BC_Rhodes_earthquake "226 BC Rhodes earthquake"), although parts of it were preserved. In accordance with a certain [oracle](Oracle "Oracle"), the Rhodians did not build it again.[[3]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-4) [John Malalas](John_Malalas "John Malalas") wrote that <Hadrian> in his reign re-erected the Colossus,[[4]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-5) but he was mistaken.[[5]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-6) According to the <Suda>, the Rhodians were called Colossaeans (Κολοσσαεῖς), because they erected the statue on the island.[[6]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-7)

In 653, an Arab force under Muslim general [Mu'awiya I](Mu'awiya_I "Mu'awiya I") conquered Rhodes, and according to the Chronicle of [Theophanes the Confessor](Theophanes_the_Confessor "Theophanes the Confessor"),[[7]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-ReferenceA-8) the statue was completely destroyed and the remains sold;[[8]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-Clarendon_Press_–_Oxford-9) this account may be unreliable.[[9]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-conrad-10)

Since 2008, a series of as-yet-unrealized proposals to build a new Colossus at Rhodes Harbour have been announced, although the actual location of the original monument remains in dispute.[[10]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-Guardian-11)[[11]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-pop_mechs-12)

## Siege of Rhodes

Main article: [Siege of Rhodes (305–304 BC)](Siege_of_Rhodes_(305%E2%80%93304_BC) "Siege of Rhodes (305–304 BC)")

In the early fourth century BC, Rhodes, allied with [Ptolemy I of Egypt](Ptolemy_I_Soter "Ptolemy I Soter"), prevented a mass invasion staged by their common enemy, [Antigonus I Monophthalmus](Antigonus_I_Monophthalmus "Antigonus I Monophthalmus").

In 304 BC a relief force of ships sent by Ptolemy arrived, and [Demetrius](Demetrius_I_of_Macedon "Demetrius I of Macedon") (son of Antigonus) and his army abandoned the siege, leaving behind most of their siege equipment. To celebrate their victory, the Rhodians sold the equipment left behind for 300 [talents](Attic_talent "Attic talent")[[12]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-13) and decided to use the money to build a colossal statue of their patron god, <Helios>. Construction was left to the direction of [Chares](Chares_of_Lindos "Chares of Lindos"), a native of Lindos in Rhodes, who had been involved with large-scale statues before. His teacher, the sculptor <Lysippos>, had constructed a 22-metre-high (72-foot)[[13]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-14) bronze statue of <Zeus> at [Tarentum](Taranto "Taranto").

## Construction

Construction began in 292 BC. Ancient accounts, which differ to some degree, describe the structure as being built with iron tie bars to which brass plates were fixed to form the skin. The interior of the structure, which stood on a 15-metre-high (49-foot) white [marble](Marble "Marble") [pedestal](Pedestal "Pedestal") near the Rhodes harbour entrance, was then filled with stone blocks as construction progressed.[[14]](Colossus_of_Rhodes#cite_note-15) Other sources place the Colossus on a breakwater in the harbour. The **Lighthouse of Alexandria**, sometimes called the **Pharos of Alexandria** (/ˈfɛərɒs/ *FAIR-oss*; [Ancient Greek](Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): ὁ Φάρος τῆς Ἀλεξανδρείας, [romanized](Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *ho Pháros tês Alexandreías*, [contemporary Koine](Koine_Greek_phonology#Learned_pronunciation,_4th_century_BCE_until_early_Roman_period "Koine Greek phonology") Greek pronunciation: [ho pʰáros tɛ̂ːs aleksandrěːaːs]; [Arabic](Arabic_language "Arabic language"): فنار الإسكندرية), was a [lighthouse](Lighthouse "Lighthouse") built by the [Ptolemaic Kingdom](Ptolemaic_Kingdom "Ptolemaic Kingdom") of [Ancient Egypt](Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt"), during the reign of [Ptolemy II Philadelphus](Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus "Ptolemy II Philadelphus") (280–247 BC).[[2]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-2) It has been estimated to have been at least 100 metres (330 ft) in overall height.[[3]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-3) One of the [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World"), for many centuries it was one of the [tallest man-made structures in the world](Tallest_man-made_structures_in_the_world "Tallest man-made structures in the world").

The lighthouse was severely damaged by three earthquakes between 956 and 1323 AD and became an abandoned ruin. It was the third-longest surviving ancient wonder, after the [Mausoleum at Halicarnassus](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus "Mausoleum at Halicarnassus") and the extant [Great Pyramid of Giza](Great_Pyramid_of_Giza "Great Pyramid of Giza"), surviving in part until 1480, when the last of its remnant stones were used to build the [Citadel of Qaitbay](Citadel_of_Qaitbay "Citadel of Qaitbay") on the site.

In 1994, a team of French archaeologists dove into the water of Alexandria's Eastern Harbour and discovered some remains of the lighthouse on the sea floor.[[4]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-NovaTrans-4) In 2016 the [Ministry of State of Antiquities](Ministry_of_State_of_Antiquities "Ministry of State of Antiquities") in Egypt had plans to turn submerged ruins of ancient Alexandria, including those of the Pharos, into an underwater [museum](Museum "Museum").[[5]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-5)

## Origin

Pharos was a small island located on the western edge of the [Nile Delta](Nile_Delta "Nile Delta"). In 332 BC [Alexander the Great](Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great") founded the city of <Alexandria> on an [isthmus](Isthmus "Isthmus") opposite Pharos. Alexandria and Pharos were later connected by a [mole](Mole_(architecture) "Mole (architecture)")[[6]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-EverymansSCD-6) spanning more than 1,200 metres (0.75 miles), which was called the *<Heptastadion>* ("seven stadia"—a *[stadion](Stadion_(unit) "Stadion (unit)")* was a Greek [unit of length](Unit_of_length "Unit of length") measuring approximately 180 m).
The etymology of "Pharos" is uncertain. The word became generalized in modern Greek (φάρος 'fáros'), and was borrowed by Italian and Spanish ('faro') and French ('phare').

The east side of the mole became the Great Harbour, now an open bay; on the west side lay the port of Eunostos, with its inner basin Kibotos now vastly enlarged to form the modern harbour. Today's city development lying between the present Grand Square and the modern Ras el-Tin quarter is built on the silt which gradually widened and obliterated this mole. The Ras el-Tin promontory, where [Ras el-Tin Palace](Ras_el-Tin_Palace "Ras el-Tin Palace") was built in the 19th century, represents all that is left of the island of Pharos,[[7]](Lighthouse_of_Alexandria#cite_note-7) the site of the lighthouse at its eastern point having been weathered away by the sea.

The **Mausoleum at Halicarnassus** or **Tomb of Mausolus**[[lower-alpha 1]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-1) ([Ancient Greek](Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Μαυσωλεῖον τῆς Ἁλικαρνασσοῦ; [Turkish](Turkish_language "Turkish language"): *Halikarnas Mozolesi*) was a tomb built between 353 and 350 BC in <Halicarnassus> (present <Bodrum>, <Turkey>) for <Mausolus>, an Anatolian from <Caria> and a [satrap](Satrap "Satrap") in the [Achaemenid Empire](Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire"), and his [sister-wife](Sister-wife "Sister-wife") [Artemisia II of Caria](Artemisia_II_of_Caria "Artemisia II of Caria"). The structure was designed by the [Greek](Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") [architects](Architecture_of_ancient_Greece "Architecture of ancient Greece") <Satyros> and [Pythius of Priene](Pythius_of_Priene "Pythius of Priene").[[1]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-Kostof-2)[[2]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-Gloag-3) Its elevated tomb structure is derived from the tombs of neighbouring <Lycia>, a territory Mausolus had invaded and annexed c. 360 BC, such as the [Nereid Monument](Nereid_Monument "Nereid Monument").[[3]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-André-Salvini-4)

The Mausoleum was approximately 45 m (148 ft) in height, and the four sides were adorned with [sculptural](Sculpture "Sculpture") [reliefs](Relief "Relief"), each created by one of four Greek sculptors: <Leochares>, <Bryaxis>, <Scopas> of <Paros>, and [Timotheus](Timotheus_(sculptor) "Timotheus (sculptor)").[[4]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-Smith-5) The Mausoleum contained total 400 freestanding sculptures.[[5]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-6) The mausoleum was considered to be such an aesthetic triumph that [Antipater of Sidon](Antipater_of_Sidon "Antipater of Sidon") identified it as one of his [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World"). It was destroyed by successive earthquakes from the 12th to the 15th century;[[6]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-7)[[7]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-8)[[8]](Mausoleum_at_Halicarnassus#cite_note-9) it was the last surviving of the six destroyed wonders.

The word *[mausoleum](Mausoleum "Mausoleum")* has now come to be used generically for an above-ground tomb.

## Conquest

In the 4th century BC, <Halicarnassus> was the capital of the small regional kingdom of <Caria>, within the [Achaemenid Empire](Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") on the western coast of [Asia Minor](Anatolia "Anatolia").

In 377 BC, the nominal ruler of the region, <Hecatomnus> of <Milas>, died and left control of the kingdom to his son, Mausolus. Hecatomnus, a local [dynast](Dynast "Dynast") under the Persians, took control of several of the neighboring cities and districts. After Artemisia and Mausolus, he had several other daughters and sons: [Ada](Ada_of_Caria "Ada of Caria") (adoptive mother of [Alexander the Great](Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great")), <Idrieus>, and [Pixodarus](Pixodarus_of_Caria "Pixodarus of Caria"). Mausolus extended his territory as far as the southwest coast of Anatolia, invading, in particular, the territory of <Lycia>, remarkable for its numerous monumental tombs such as the [Tombs at Xanthos](Tombs_at_Xanthos "Tombs at Xanthos"), from which he took his inspiration for his mausoleum.[[3]

For other shrines dedicated to Artemis, see [Temple of Artemis (disambiguation)](Temple_of_Artemis_(disambiguation) "Temple of Artemis (disambiguation)").

The **Temple of Artemis** or **Artemision** ([Greek](Greek_language "Greek language"): Ἀρτεμίσιον; [Turkish](Turkish_language "Turkish language"): *Artemis Tapınağı*), also known as the **Temple of Diana**, was a [Greek temple](Greek_temple "Greek temple") dedicated to an ancient, local form of the goddess <Artemis> (identified with [Diana](Diana_(mythology) "Diana (mythology)"), a [Roman goddess](Religion_in_ancient_Rome "Religion in ancient Rome")). It was located in <Ephesus> (near the modern town of [Selçuk](Sel%C3%A7uk "Selçuk") in present-day <Turkey>). By 401 AD it had been ruined or destroyed.[[1]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-1) Only foundations and fragments of the last temple remain at the site.

The earliest version of the temple (a [Bronze Age](Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") *[temenos](Temenos "Temenos")*) antedated the [Ionic immigration](Ionic_immigration "Ionic immigration") by many years. <Callimachus>, in his *Hymn to Artemis*, attributed it to the <Amazons>. In the 7th century BC, it was destroyed by a flood.

Its reconstruction, in more grandiose form, began around 550 BC, under <Chersiphron>, the Cretan [architect](Architect "Architect"), and his son <Metagenes>. The project was funded by <Croesus> of <Lydia>, and took 10 years to complete. This version of the temple was destroyed in 356 BC by an [arsonist](Arson "Arson").

The next, greatest, and last form of the temple, funded by the Ephesians themselves, is described in [Antipater of Sidon](Antipater_of_Sidon "Antipater of Sidon")'s list of the world's [Seven Wonders](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World"):
> I have set eyes on the wall of lofty <Babylon> on which is a road for chariots, and the [statue of Zeus by the Alpheus](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia "Statue of Zeus at Olympia"), and the [hanging gardens](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon "Hanging Gardens of Babylon"), and the [colossus of the Sun](Colossus_of_Rhodes "Colossus of Rhodes"), and the huge labour of the [high pyramids](Egyptian_pyramids "Egyptian pyramids"), and the vast [tomb of Mausolus](Mausoleum_of_Mausolus "Mausoleum of Mausolus"); but when I saw the house of Artemis that mounted to the clouds, those other marvels lost their brilliancy, and I said, "Lo, apart from Olympus, the Sun never looked on aught so grand".[[2]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-2)

## Location and history

The Temple of Artemis (*Artemision*) was located near the ancient city of Ephesus, about 75 kilometres (47 mi) south from the modern port city of [İzmir](%C4%B0zmir "İzmir"), in Turkey. Today the site lies on the edge of the modern town of [Selçuk](Sel%C3%A7uk "Selçuk").

The sacred site (*[temenos](Temenos "Temenos")*) at Ephesus was far older than the *Artemision* itself. [Pausanias](Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)") was certain that it antedated the Ionic immigration by many years, being older even than the oracular shrine of <Apollo> at <Didyma>.[[3]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-3) He said that the pre-Ionic inhabitants of the city were <Leleges> and [Lydians](Lydia "Lydia"). <Callimachus>, in his *Hymn to Artemis* attributed the earliest *temenos* at Ephesus to the <Amazons>, legendary warrior-women whose religious practise he imagined already centered upon an image (*bretas*) of Artemis, their matron goddess. Pausanias believed that the temple pre-dated the Amazons.[[4]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-4)

Pausanias's estimation of the site's antiquity seems well-founded. Before World War I, site excavations by [David George Hogarth](David_George_Hogarth "David George Hogarth") seemed to identify three successive temple buildings. Re-excavations in 1987–88 and re-appraisal of Hogarth's account [[5]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-5) confirmed that the site was occupied as early as the [Bronze Age](Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"), with a sequence of pottery finds that extend forward to [Middle Geometric times](Geometric_art "Geometric art"), when a [peripteral](Peripteral "Peripteral") temple with a floor of hard-packed clay was constructed in the second half of the 8th century BC.[[6]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-6) The peripteral temple at Ephesus offers the earliest example of a peripteral type on the coast of Asia Minor, and perhaps the earliest Greek temple surrounded by colonnades anywhere.

In the 7th century BC, a flood[[7]](Temple_of_Artemis#cite_note-7) destroyed the temple, depositing over half a meter of sand and flotsam over the original clay floor. The **Statue of Zeus at Olympia** was a giant seated figure, about 12.4 m (41 ft) tall,[[1]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-1) made by the Greek sculptor <Phidias> around 435 BC at the sanctuary of [Olympia, Greece](Olympia%2C_Greece "Olympia, Greece"), and erected in the [Temple of Zeus](Temple_of_Zeus%2C_Olympia "Temple of Zeus, Olympia") there. <Zeus> is the [sky](Sky_father "Sky father") and [thunder god](Thunder_god "Thunder god") in [ancient Greek religion](Ancient_Greek_religion "Ancient Greek religion"), who rules as [king of the gods](King_of_the_gods "King of the gods") of [Mount Olympus](Mount_Olympus "Mount Olympus").

The statue was a [chryselephantine sculpture](Chryselephantine_sculpture "Chryselephantine sculpture") of ivory plates and gold panels on a wooden framework. Zeus sat on a painted cedarwood throne ornamented with ebony, ivory, gold, and precious stones. It was one of the [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World").

The statue was lost and destroyed before the end of the 5th century AD, with conflicting accounts of the date and circumstances. Details of its form are known only from ancient Greek descriptions and representations on coins.

## History

The statue of Zeus was commissioned by the <Eleans>, custodians of the [Olympic Games](Ancient_Olympics "Ancient Olympics"), in the latter half of the fifth century BC for their newly constructed [Temple of Zeus](Temple_of_Zeus%2C_Olympia "Temple of Zeus, Olympia"). Seeking to outdo their Athenian rivals, the Eleans employed sculptor <Phidias>, who had previously made the massive statue of [Athena Parthenos](Athena_Parthenos "Athena Parthenos") in the <Parthenon>.[[2]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-2)

The statue occupied half the width of the aisle of the temple built to house it. The geographer <Strabo> noted early in the 1st century BC that the statue gave "the impression that if Zeus arose and stood erect he would unroof the temple."[[3]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-3) The *Zeus* was a [chryselephantine sculpture](Chryselephantine_sculpture "Chryselephantine sculpture"), made with ivory and gold panels on a wooden substructure. No copy in marble or bronze has survived, though there are recognizable but only approximate versions on coins of nearby [Elis](Elis_(city) "Elis (city)") and on Roman coins and [engraved gems](Engraved_gem "Engraved gem").[[4]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-4)

The 2nd-century AD geographer and traveler [Pausanias](Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)") left a detailed description: the statue was crowned with a sculpted wreath of olive sprays and wore a gilded robe made from glass and carved with animals and lilies. Its right hand held a small chryselephantine statue of crowned [Nike](Nike_(mythology) "Nike (mythology)"), goddess of victory; its left a scepter inlaid with many metals, supporting an eagle. The throne featured painted figures and wrought images and was decorated with gold, precious stones, ebony, and ivory.[[5]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-5) Zeus' golden sandals rested upon a footstool decorated with an <Amazonomachy> in relief. The passage underneath the throne was restricted by painted screens.[[6]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-McWilliamPuttock2011-6)

Pausanias also recounts that the statue was kept constantly coated with olive oil to counter the harmful effect on the ivory caused by the "marshiness" of the <Altis> grove. The floor in front of the image was paved with black tiles and surrounded by a raised rim of marble to contain the oil.[[7]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-Paus-7) This reservoir acted as a [reflecting pool](Reflecting_pool "Reflecting pool") which doubled the apparent height of the statue.[[8]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-8)

According to the Roman historian <Livy>, the Roman general [Aemilius Paullus](Lucius_Aemilius_Paullus_Macedonicus "Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus") (the victor over <Macedon>) saw the statue and "was moved to his soul, as if he had seen the god in person",[[9]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-9) while the 1st-century AD Greek orator [Dio Chrysostom](Dio_Chrysostom "Dio Chrysostom") declared that a single glimpse of the statue would make a man forget all his earthly troubles.[[10]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-10)

According to <Strabo>, when Phidias was asked about the model he would used for his Zeus, he answered that he would portray Zeus according to these words of <Homer>:[[11]](Statue_of_Zeus_at_Olympia#cite_note-11)
> The son of Cronos spoke, and bowed his dark brow in assent, and the ambrosial locks waved from the king's immortal head; and he made great Olympus quake (English translation by A.T. Murray

For other uses, see [Hanging Garden (disambiguation)](Hanging_Garden_(disambiguation) "Hanging Garden (disambiguation)").

The **Hanging Gardens of Babylon** were one of the [Seven Wonders of the Ancient World](Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World") listed by [Hellenic](Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") culture. They were described as a remarkable feat of engineering with an ascending series of tiered gardens containing a wide variety of trees, shrubs, and vines, resembling a large green mountain constructed of mud bricks. It was said to have been built in the ancient city of <Babylon>, near present-day <Hillah>, [Babil](Babil_Governorate "Babil Governorate") province, in <Iraq>. The Hanging Gardens' name is derived from the Greek word κρεμαστός (*kremastós*, lit. (literal translation) 'overhanging'), which has a broader meaning than the modern English word "hanging" and refers to trees being planted on a raised structure such as a [terrace](Terrace_(building) "Terrace (building)").[[1]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-Dalley1993-1)[[2]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-Reade2000-2)[[3]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-Foster2004-3)

According to one legend, the Hanging Gardens were built alongside a grand palace known as *The Marvel of Mankind*, by the [Neo-Babylonian](Neo-Babylonian_Empire "Neo-Babylonian Empire") King [Nebuchadnezzar II](Nebuchadnezzar_II "Nebuchadnezzar II") (who ruled between 605 and 562 BC), for his [Median](Medes "Medes") wife, [Queen Amytis](Amytis_of_Babylon "Amytis of Babylon"), because she missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland. This was attested to by the Babylonian priest <Berossus>, writing in about 290 BC, a description that was later quoted by <Josephus>. The construction of the Hanging Gardens has also been attributed to the legendary queen <Semiramis>[[4]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-UN1998-4) and they have been called the *Hanging Gardens of Semiramis* as an alternative name.[[5]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-AE2018-5)

The Hanging Gardens are the only one of the Seven Wonders for which the location has not been definitively established.[[6]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-autogenerated1988-6) There are no extant Babylonian texts that mention the gardens, and no definitive archaeological evidence has been found in Babylon.[[7]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-7)[[8]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-8) Three theories have been suggested to account for this: first, that they were purely mythical, and the descriptions found in ancient Greek and Roman writings (including those of <Strabo>, [Diodorus Siculus](Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus") and [Quintus Curtius Rufus](Quintus_Curtius_Rufus "Quintus Curtius Rufus")) represented a romantic ideal of an eastern garden;[[9]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-9) second, that they existed in Babylon, but were destroyed sometime around the first century AD;[[10]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-10)[[4]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-UN1998-4) and third, that the legend refers to a well-documented garden that the [Assyrian](Assyria "Assyria") King <Sennacherib> (704–681 BC) built in his capital city of <Nineveh> on the River <Tigris>, near the modern city of <Mosul>.[[11]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-11)[[1]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-Dalley1993-1)

## Descriptions in classical literature

There are five principal writers whose descriptions of Babylon exist in some form today. These writers concern themselves with the size of the Hanging Gardens, their overall design and means of [irrigation](Irrigation "Irrigation"), and why they were built.

<Josephus> (c. 37–100 AD) quotes a description of the gardens by <Berossus>, a Babylonian priest of <Marduk>,[[6]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-autogenerated1988-6) whose writing c. 290 BC is the earliest known mention of the gardens.[[5]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-AE2018-5) Berossus described the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II and is the only source to credit that king with the construction of the Hanging Gardens.[[12]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-12)[[13]](Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon#cite_note-Dalley1994-13)

Based on my research, here are the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World** and their primary construction materials:

## 1. Great Pyramid of Giza (Egypt)
- **Primary Materials:** Limestone, granite, and mortar
- The pyramid was built using an estimated 2.3 million large blocks, weighing 6 million tonnes total. The outer casing was made of smooth white limestone from the Tura region, while the interior chambers used granite. Local limestone from the Giza Plateau formed the core structure.
- **Status:** Still standing (the only wonder to survive to modern times)

## 2. Colossus of Rhodes (Greece)
- **Primary Materials:** Bronze plates, iron tie bars, and marble (pedestal)
- The statue stood approximately 33 meters (108 feet) tall. Ancient accounts describe it as being built with iron tie bars to which brass plates were fixed to form the skin. The interior was filled with stone blocks as construction progressed. It stood on a 15-meter high white marble pedestal.
- **Status:** Destroyed by an earthquake in 226 BC

## 3. Lighthouse of Alexandria (Egypt)
- **Primary Materials:** Stone and masonry
- Built between 284-246 BC, the lighthouse stood at least 100 meters (330 feet) tall. It had three tiers: square at the bottom, octagonal in the middle, and cylindrical at the top. It was constructed using stone masonry.
- **Status:** Destroyed by earthquakes between 956-1323 AD

## 4. Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (Turkey)
- **Primary Materials:** Marble
- This tomb was built between 353-350 BC and stood approximately 45 meters (148 feet) tall. It featured elaborate sculptural reliefs created by four Greek sculptors. The structure was adorned with marble and contained 400 freestanding sculptures.
- **Status:** Destroyed by earthquakes from the 12th to 15th centuries

## 5. Temple of Artemis (Turkey)
- **Primary Materials:** Marble
- Located in Ephesus, this temple was funded by Croesus of Lydia and took 10 years to complete (around 550 BC). It was destroyed by arson in 356 BC and later rebuilt. The temple featured marble columns and extensive decorative elements.
- **Status:** Destroyed in 401 AD

## 6. Statue of Zeus at Olympia (Greece)
- **Primary Materials:** Ivory, gold, cedar wood, ebony, and precious stones
- Created around 435 BC by the sculptor Phidias, this was a *chryselephantine* sculpture (ivory plates and gold panels on a wooden framework). Zeus sat on a painted cedarwood throne ornamented with ebony, ivory, gold, and precious stones. The throne featured painted figures and wrought images decorated with gold, precious stones, ebony, and ivory.
- **Status:** Destroyed before the end of the 5th century AD

## 7. Hanging Gardens of Babylon (Iraq)
- **Primary Materials:** Mud bricks, stone pillars, and plants
- These tiered gardens were described as resembling "a large green mountain constructed of mud bricks." According to ancient sources, the gardens had very high walls supported by stone pillars. The exact location and existence of the gardens remains debated by historians.
- **Status:** Debated (no definitive archaeological evidence found)

functions.name: fork
functions.desc: Delegate a subtask to a helper agent. Use join(id) to get a helper's result.         You can call this multiple times to take multiple actions. Do not delegate the entire task you were given.         If the user's query can be resolved in parallel, call this multiple times then use join("all").

json_schema.description: Delegate a subtask to a helper agent. Use join(id) to get a helper's result.         You can call this multiple times to take multiple actions. Do not delegate the entire task you were given.         If the user's query can be resolved in parallel, call this multiple times then use join("all").

instructions.description: Detailed instructions on what your helper should do to help you. This should include all the information the helper needs.

json_schema.title: fork

functions.name: join
functions.desc: Wait for spawned helper agents to complete and retrieve their results.         Pass the agent IDs returned by `fork`, "all", or "next".         Returns the final responses from each agent.

json_schema.description: Wait for spawned helper agents to complete and retrieve their results.         Pass the agent IDs returned by `fork`, "all", or "next".         Returns the final responses from each agent.

id.description: The id of the subagent. Pass "next" for the next helper, or "all" for all running subagents.

json_schema.title: join
